This page runs no code. It says why a tuned model's own score cannot be
trusted, which quantity the nested number describes, and how to read its
standard error. It also covers fold disagreement and when nesting is worth
its cost. The worked example is `vignette("nested-cv")`.

## The case for nesting

When you tune with cross-validation, you try several settings, the
candidates, and keep the one with the best score. Scores are noisy, and the
best of several noisy numbers tends to look better than it is. So the
winner's score overstates what the model will do on new data, by an amount
nothing in the output reveals. That is why the results object this package
returns, and the final fit built from it, both refuse tune's ranking
functions such as `show_best()`.

At a small sample size the noise is large, so the winner's score may not
even look better than an honest one. Distrust it for how it was chosen, not
for which way it is off.

Nested cross-validation scores the whole tuning procedure, meaning every
step you run on the data: resample, tune, pick a setting, fit. Nesting puts
that procedure inside a second, outer resampling loop. Each outer fold tunes
from scratch on its own analysis rows, fits the chosen setting there, and
scores that fit once on assessment rows the tuning never saw. The mean of
those outer scores is the estimate.

The number `collect_metrics()` reports describes the whole tune-and-fit
procedure: resample, tune, select, fit. That is the number to report. The
model fitted at the end for deployment is a separate object, and it has no
performance number of its own. Everything computable from its training data
was used up in selecting and fitting it.

## The quantity estimated

Bayle et al. (2026) call the quantity the k-fold test error of the
procedure. It is the error of running those four steps on the training rows
each outer fold saw, then predicting fresh data drawn like the training
data.

Four things it is not. It is not the error of the deployed model, which is
built afterwards on all the rows and estimated by nothing here. It says
nothing about whether the deployed model's parameter values are the right
ones. It is not about a different population or sample size. And it is not that error averaged over every
training set you might have drawn, which would describe the method rather
than this data. Luo and Barber (2026) prove
that any assumption-free test of that averaged quantity needs a dataset
many times larger than the training set. So this package offers none.

## A slight pessimism

The number tends to look a little worse than the procedure deserves. Every
outer fold trains on its analysis rows only, so every model scored is built
on less data than the model you finally deploy. Less data usually means
worse predictions. Varma and Simon (2006) separate this training-size
effect, which can go either way, from the selection effect, which is always
optimistic.

Varma and Simon (2006) ran nested cross-validation on null data with 40
samples, where the true error is 50.0%, and got 54.2%. They attribute the
4.2-point overshoot to training on 39 rows rather than 40. Wilimitis and
Walsh (2023) compared methods on 41,121 hospital visits against a held-out
benchmark. Nested cross-validation was among the most pessimistic, by
roughly 1 to 2% of AUROC and 5 to 9% of AUPR. The same study reports one
cell where the nested estimate came out optimistic instead.

The gap is a property of the estimator, not a prediction about any one run.
It is never a licence to adjust the reported figure upward.

## The standard error

`std_err` is the standard error of the mean across the outer folds. It is
the standard deviation of the fold scores divided by the square root of
their number. It is not the fold-to-fold spread, which is larger by that
factor. `collect_metrics(res, summarize = FALSE)` gives the per-fold scores.
It is also not a confidence interval. This package ships no inference on the
nested estimate.

## Comparing two workflows

Suppose you run the loop on two workflows and one comes back lower. Nothing
in the output says whether the difference is real, because there is no
valid interval to subtract. Bayle et al. (2026) give a sharper reason not
to build one. A cross-validation interval for one procedure is valid when
that procedure is stable. The difference between two procedures can fail
that condition even when each procedure meets it. The failure is worst when
the two procedures are similar. A gap between two nested estimates is a reason to look
closer, never a result.

The same holds for a set of workflows run through one design with
`nested_workflow_map()`. Picking the workflow with the best estimate is a
selection step the outer loop did not nest. So the package offers no
ranking or best-workflow function for the set.

## Disagreement between folds

When the folds split over a parameter, the data does not pick its value
clearly. Whichever value the
final model carries was not strongly preferred by the evidence. That is not
a defect in the estimate, which already averages over this variability. It
is a defect in any story about the selected parameters being the right
ones.

Disagreement is expected wherever the candidates perform about equally
well. As two candidates' predictions converge, which of them wins any
particular fold becomes close to a coin flip (Bayle et al., 2026).

## The cost of nesting

Whether nesting pays depends on how much room the selection step had to
overfit. Tibshirani and Tibshirani (2009) measured that room on pure noise,
where the true error rate is 0.5. With 400 observations and 100 features,
the tuned score was under 3 points too good. With 40 observations and 1000
features, the lowest tuned score read 0.384, 11.6 points too good. Even
there the learner mattered: an SVM was 2.5 points too good and a tree only
0.2. That paper's remedy is
a correction, not nesting. In short, the bias is largest with wide data, a
big grid, and a preprocessing step the loop has to redo.

Nesting removes little when the data is tall and the search is small. Wilimitis
and Walsh (2023) ran that case, 41,121 visits and a modest grid. Nesting
bought nothing but the pessimism above, at a cost that grew quadratically in
the fold count. Their advice, and this package's, is to nest when the
feature space is wide relative to the sample, the search covers many
algorithms and parameters, and the compute is affordable.

Small data is not safe without nesting. Vabalas et al. (2019) simulated
pure noise, where the honest accuracy is 50%. Cross-validation without
nesting still reported better than chance at a sample size of 1000. Nested
cross-validation was indistinguishable from chance at 96.5% of the sample
sizes tested. The bias thins with sample size and does not disappear.

## Feature selection inside the workflow

Vabalas et al. (2019) also compared two mistakes: leaving feature selection
outside the loop, and leaving parameter tuning outside it. The first was far
more damaging. The loop here re-estimates the whole workflow inside every
fold. So if your pipeline selects features, put that step in the recipe
inside the workflow you pass in. Anything done to the data before the call
is not re-estimated. No result here can tell that it happened.

comparison with cross-validation. *arXiv:2508.04409*.

Luo, Y., & Barber, R. F. (2026). The limits of assumption-free tests for
algorithm performance. *Bernoulli*, 32(3), 2427–2450.

error rate in cross-validation. *The Annals of Applied Statistics*, 3(2),

examples of cross-validation for model development and evaluation in health
